column1: # Where each German noun's gender in lex-de.tsv was read.
# The tooltip prints a noun's gender beside it, der, die or das being the
# first thing a learner says. On 2026-10-08 every German noun was read
# against English Wiktionary's German entry, fetched raw, and none was
# wrong: 167 of the 178 rows carry the gender of their page's one German
# noun, and the 11 others were read by sense.
# A Wiktionary page holds every word of one spelling, so a line citing it
# means the gender of this word's own noun there. Eight pages hold more than
# one: der See, lake, beside die See, sea; der Schild, shield, beside das
# Schild, sign; der Hut, hat, beside die Hut, guard; der Morgen, morning,
# beside das Morgen, tomorrow; der Mund, mouth, beside an obsolete feminine
# Mund, protection; der Bauer, farmer, beside der or das Bauer, a birdcage;
# der Ort, place, beside obsolete and mining nouns of either gender; and
# die Hand beside a football clipping of Handspiel.
# Where Wiktionary gives one word two genders, the seed's is one of them, as
# the Old English and French ledgers have it: Monat, month, is masculine or
# neuter, and Wurm, worm, neuter only when it means "baby, mite". Fremder,
# stranger, is an adjective used as a noun, and the strong form the seed
# writes, ein Fremder, is the masculine one.
# tests/tools/genders.test.ts requires every noun in lex-de.tsv to have a
# line here giving the gender the seed gives, citing the noun's own entry,
# and fails on a line outliving its noun.
